problem: Prior zero-shot ObjectNav methods that pick frontiers semantically (ESC, LGX, SemUtil) first turn visual observations into text with an object detector, then reason over those labels with an LLM or BERT. That text step is a bottleneck and throws away visual cues such as room type, lighting and layout. LLMs may also need a remote server. Task-trained ObjectNav policies, by contrast, are limited to closed object sets and are trained only in simulation.
motivation: Humans use visual semantic cues directly to decide where to search for an object in an unfamiliar building. A vision-language model can score how promising an RGB view is for a text-specified target without going through text, and it runs on a laptop. Grounding these scores in space and using them to rank exploration frontiers should give efficient, open-vocabulary, training-free semantic search that can be deployed on real robots.
key_idea: Build a top-down, language-grounded value map by projecting BLIP-2 image-text cosine similarities (RGB image vs. 'Seems like there is a <target> ahead.') into the camera's view cone. Fuse overlapping observations with confidence weights, then explore the frontier with the highest value until an open-vocabulary detector finds the target.
insight: Vision-language similarity on raw RGB, grounded spatially on a map, is a strong enough semantic prior for frontier selection to beat detector-to-text LLM/BERT pipelines and even several task-trained ObjectNav policies. How the value map fuses repeated views matters. In Table II, confidence-weighted averaging (confidence falls off as cos² from the optical axis) beats plain averaging, and overwriting with the newest value hurts most: HM3D SR 52.5 vs 51.8 vs 44.5, Gibson SR 84.0 vs 83.0 vs 76.1. Failure analysis shows much of the remaining gap is structural rather than semantic: 14.6% of HM3D and 9.6% of MP3D episodes fail because the target is on another floor. Lower scan quality in MP3D also depresses results there.
method: Frontier map: depth is converted to a point cloud, points too short or too tall to be obstacles are filtered out, and the rest are projected with odometry onto a 2D obstacle/explored grid. The midpoint of each explored/unexplored boundary becomes a candidate frontier waypoint. An episode starts with a full 360° spin to initialize the maps, and the agent calls STOP (unsuccessfully) if no frontiers remain.

Language-grounded value map: BLIP-2 computes an image-text cosine similarity between the current RGB frame and the prompt 'Seems like there is a <target object> ahead.' This score is written into a semantic-value channel over the camera's top-down FOV cone, masked by depth occlusion.

Confidence channel and fusion: each cell's confidence is cos²(θ/(θ_fov/2)·π/2), where θ is the angle from the optical axis. Revisited cells get v_new=(c_curr·v_curr+c_prev·v_prev)/(c_curr+c_prev) and c_new=(c_curr²+c_prev²)/(c_curr+c_prev).
Frontier selection: each frontier is scored by the value map, and the highest-valued frontier becomes the next waypoint.

Object detection and goal localization: YOLOv7 handles COCO-class targets and Grounding-DINO handles all other categories. Mobile-SAM extracts the object contour from the box, and depth gives the closest point on the object as the goal waypoint. STOP is called once the robot is within the success radius.

Waypoint navigation: a depth-plus-relative-goal PointNav policy (no RGB) is trained with VER (distributed RL) on HM3D train scenes for 2.5B steps (4 GPUs, 64 workers each, ~7 days). It navigates to both frontier and object waypoints. On the real robot it is replaced by the Boston Dynamics API, with ZoeDepth estimating depth for the gripper camera.

setting.backbone: BLIP-2 (frozen, image-text similarity) + YOLOv7 / Grounding-DINO + Mobile-SAM (frozen) for semantics; depth-only PointNav policy trained with VER RL for low-level control
setting.training_data: No ObjectNav/semantic-navigation training (zero-shot). Only the low-level PointNav policy is trained, with VER RL on the HM3D train split for 2.5B steps. Other models are off-the-shelf pre-trained.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D + odometry (pose relative to start)
setting.action_space: low-level MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30° / LOOK_UP/DOWN 30° / STOP, produced by a PointNav policy toward selected frontier or object waypoints
setting.privileged: none (odometry sensor only; no pre-built map)

results: VLFM sets the best SPL on all three ObjectNav benchmarks: Gibson 52.2 SPL / 84.0 SR, HM3D 30.4 / 52.5, MP3D 17.5 / 36.4. Among zero-shot methods it beats SemUtil on Gibson by +11.7 SPL / +14.7 SR and ESC on HM3D by +8.1 / +13.3 and on MP3D by +3.3 / +7.7. It also beats trained methods: SemExp on Gibson (+19.2 SPL) and PONI on MP3D (+5.4 SPL). The only method with higher SR is PIRLNav on HM3D (64.1 vs 52.5, trained on 77k human demos), and VLFM still has higher SPL there (+3.3).
limitations: Single-floor only: odometry lacks a z coordinate, so maps cannot be reset across floors. This causes failure on 14.6% of HM3D and 9.6% of MP3D episodes that require stairs.
Assumes targets are visible from the default camera height, with no active camera control or manipulation-based search (e.g., opening drawers).
The value map is target-specific, so it cannot be reused for sequential multi-object search or for language-specified tasks like VLN.
